stem: A 6-month-old girl has persistent oral thrush, chronic diarrhea and poor weight gain. While abroad she received a live oral poliovirus vaccine. Ten days later she develops asymmetric flaccid weakness of the right leg. Stool testing grows a vaccine-derived poliovirus. Her sibling received the same vaccine and is well.
oneliner: 6F + thrush, chronic diarrhea, poor growth + live oral polio vaccine → 10 d later asymmetric flaccid leg weakness, vaccine-strain virus in stool, healthy sibling → why?
ask: Which of the following best explains why she developed disease from the vaccine?

options.A: Contamination of the vaccine with wild-type virus
options.B: Molecular mimicry between viral and neuronal antigens
options.C: Attenuated virus replicated unchecked because of her defective cellular immunity
options.D: Exotoxin released by the vaccine virus

whyNot.A: **Her sibling got the same vaccine** and is well, so the vaccine itself was not the cause
whyNot.B: **Autoimmune cross-reaction** (like Guillain-Barre); here the vaccine virus itself is in her stool
whyNot.D: **Polioviruses make no exotoxin**; damage comes from viral replication in motor neurons
whyNot.E: **Type III reaction** would cause serum sickness, not flaccid paralysis

answer: Attenuated virus replicated unchecked because of her defective cellular immunity
why: **Live attenuated vaccine + persistent thrush and failure to thrive (T-cell defect)** = the weakened virus is not controlled and can cause **vaccine-associated paralytic disease**; live vaccines are avoided in immunocompromised people.

bug.name: Poliovirus (live attenuated Sabin strain)
bug.lab: Stool or throat culture, RT-PCR with sequencing to separate vaccine from wild strain
bug.virulence: Infects anterior horn motor neurons; vaccine strains can replicate unchecked in immunodeficiency or revert
bug.causes: Poliomyelitis with flaccid paralysis; vaccine-associated paralytic polio
